title: New DHS Rule Caps J-1 Visa Stays at Four Years, Disrupting Doctor Training Programs
excerpt: The finalized regulation replaces decades-old 'duration of status' flexibility with fixed admission periods, forcing nearly 17,000 foreign physicians in U.S. residencies to seek annual extensions.
body:
• DHS has finalized a rule eliminating "duration of status" for F, J, and I visa holders, replacing it with a four-year cap effective September 15, 2026.
  • Nearly 17,000 physicians on J-1 visas — many of them Indian — face mid-training disruptions as surgical and subspecialty programs routinely exceed four years.
  • Medical organizations including the AHA and AMA warn the change could worsen physician shortages and compromise patient care in underserved areas.

The Department of Homeland Security finalized a regulation on July 16 that eliminates the long-standing "duration of status" system for international students, exchange visitors, and foreign journalists, replacing it with fixed admission periods capped at four years. The rule, set to take effect on September 15, is expected to land hardest on the roughly 17,000 foreign physicians training in U.S. residency and fellowship programs on J-1 visas — a group disproportionately composed of Indian medical graduates.

Under the previous framework, in place since 1978, J-1 physicians were admitted for the entire length of their training programs. Their sponsor organization, Intealth, continuously monitored compliance and reported status updates to the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS). The new rule severs that link between visa duration and program length, requiring physicians in programs longer than four years to apply directly to USCIS for annual extensions of stay.

A Mismatch With Medical Training Timelines

The four-year cap collides with the reality of American medical education. Surgical residencies typically run five years at minimum. Primary care pathways — internal medicine followed by subspecialty fellowships in geriatrics or cardiology — routinely stretch beyond four years. Even physicians in shorter programs can be pushed past the cap by temporary leaves or remediation periods.

"For nearly half a century, the outdated 'duration of status' system has compromised national security and created an environment ripe for immigration fraud."

— Markwayne Mullin, DHS Secretary

Medical organizations see it differently. The American Hospital Association urged DHS to exempt J-1 physicians entirely, arguing the existing oversight system "has a long track record" of preventing visa misuse. The AHA warned that USCIS processing times for extension applications currently range from six to 19 months — far too slow for residency programs that issue annual contract renewals just three to five months before each academic year begins on July 1.

"Elimination of duration of status will create an untenable situation for J-1 physicians, teaching hospitals, and the patients they serve," the American Medical Association wrote in its own letter opposing the change. A coalition of 42 national health organizations has also called on DHS to either maintain the current system or align admission periods with the full planned length of each physician's training.

Patient Care at Stake

The concern extends beyond paperwork. J-1 physicians fill residency slots that would otherwise go unfilled, according to the AHA, and they disproportionately train in high-need specialties such as internal medicine, pediatrics, and family medicine. Many serve in rural and underserved communities where physician shortages are already acute.

If extension delays force physicians to leave the country mid-program, hospitals could face staffing gaps that directly affect patient care continuity. The American Board of Internal Medicine warned that the rule "converts routine educational adjustments into immigration adjudication events with the potential for prolonged disruption."

Broader Reach Beyond Medicine

The rule affects all J-1 exchange visitors — roughly 500,000 people — along with approximately 1.2 million F-1 international students and about 1,500 foreign journalists on I visas. Journalists will face a 240-day cap, reduced to 90 days for Chinese nationals.

For F-1 students, the regulation also halves the post-graduation grace period from 60 days to 30 and shifts extension authority from universities to federal immigration officials. Current visa holders already in the U.S. will automatically transition to the new framework, with their remaining stay capped at four years from the rule's effective date.

What Indian Graduates Should Watch

India sends the highest number of international students to the United States — approximately 330,000 during the 2023-24 academic year, according to India's Ministry of External Affairs. MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said New Delhi is monitoring the situation and remains in contact with Washington.

"As and when there are issues of difficulties which are brought to our attention, in regard to genuine travellers and students who seek support from the US, we take up those issues with the US side so as to minimise the difficulties that our people face."

— Randhir Jaiswal, MEA Spokesperson

The rule is subject to congressional review before its September implementation date. Indian physicians currently in residency or fellowship programs should consult their program's designated school official and an immigration attorney to assess whether their training timeline exceeds the four-year window and, if so, prepare extension filings well in advance of the deadline.
nri_angle: Indian physicians on J-1 visas in U.S. residency programs face mid-training disruptions, and India's 330,000 students in American universities confront tighter timelines and reduced grace periods.
